stories.headline: US strikes Iran's Qeshm Island near Strait of Hormuz; oil prices edge up
stories.summary: US forces carried out strikes on targets on Iran's Qeshm Island, with American officials quoted by CBS — the BBC's US partner — describing the action as limited and defensive. The strikes came on the eve of US midterm elections, a timing highlighted across international coverage. Oil prices rose modestly, about 0.5% in early Asian trading, as markets weighed the risk of renewed conflict and disruption to supplies moving through the Strait of Hormuz. A US official told the Associated Press that Iranian targets in the Strait of Hormuz area were hit, indicating the operation's focus on the strategic waterway rather than Iranian mainland territory. Iran's response and the wider diplomatic fallout were not detailed in the reports available.
stories.whyItMatters: The Strait of Hormuz is the world's most consequential oil chokepoint and a direct determinant of India's energy import bill, inflation and current account position. Any US–Iran escalation in West Asia therefore feeds straight into India's macroeconomic and foreign-policy calculus.

static.topic: Strait of Hormuz and Global Energy Chokepoints
static.syllabusNode: Economy — Energy Security & Infrastructure; also GS-II International Relations
static.whatIsIt: The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow waterway connecting the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea. It is the world's most important oil transit chokepoint, with a very large share of globally traded crude and petroleum products — commonly cited as roughly a fifth of world oil consumption — passing through it. Qeshm Island, Iran's largest island, sits within this strait.
static.background: Chokepoint vulnerability entered global energy discourse through the 1973 oil crisis, the 1979 Iranian Revolution, the 1980s 'Tanker War' during the Iran–Iraq conflict, and repeated Iranian threats to close the strait during successive sanctions episodes. The US Fifth Fleet, based in Bahrain, underwrites freedom of navigation in the region.
static.geography: The strait narrows to roughly 33 km at its narrowest, with shipping lanes passing through Omani and Iranian territorial waters. Iran's coast and islands — including Qeshm, Hormuz and Larak — command the northern shore.
static.socioEconomic: Disruption risk translates into an oil price premium, higher freight and insurance costs, and imported inflation for large net importers such as India, Japan and South Korea.
static.whyInNews: US strikes on Qeshm Island and adjacent Strait of Hormuz targets revived fears of supply disruption, nudging oil prices higher.
static.wayForward: For India: deepen strategic petroleum reserves, diversify crude sourcing (US, West Africa, Latin America), expand rupee-based and non-dollar settlement options, and accelerate renewables and ethanol blending to blunt import dependence.
prelimsPointers: Qeshm is Iran's largest island, located in the Strait of Hormuz in Hormozgan province.
The Strait of Hormuz links the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman; Iran lies to the north, Oman and the UAE to the south.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how chokepoint geopolitics in West Asia shapes India's energy security architecture and what hedging instruments India can deploy.

static.topic: US–Iran Relations and West Asia Security Architecture
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Bilateral, Regional and Global Groupings; Effect of Policies of Developed Countries on India's Interests
static.whatIsIt: US–Iran ties have been adversarial since the 1979 Iranian Revolution and the hostage crisis. The relationship is structured around Iran's nuclear programme, its regional proxy network, sanctions, and the security of Gulf oil routes.
static.background: Key milestones include the 2015 Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA) signed by Iran with the P5+1, the US withdrawal from it in 2018 and re-imposition of sanctions, and periodic flare-ups in the Gulf — including the 2020 killing of Iranian general Qasem Soleimani and attacks on tankers and Saudi oil facilities. The Abraham Accords normalised Israel's ties with several Arab states, reshaping regional alignments.
static.geography: West Asia spans the Persian Gulf, Gulf of Oman, Red Sea and Bab-el-Mandeb — a belt of overlapping chokepoints on which Asian economies depend.
static.socioEconomic: India hosts a large diaspora in the Gulf and receives substantial remittances; Gulf states supply a major share of India's crude and LPG. Escalation raises repatriation, remittance and energy-cost risks simultaneously.
static.whyInNews: US strikes on Iranian targets on Qeshm Island and in the Strait of Hormuz area mark a fresh escalation in the long-running confrontation.
static.wayForward: India should maintain strategic autonomy: continue calibrated engagement with both Washington and Tehran, protect Chabahar-linked connectivity interests, and strengthen Gulf evacuation and diaspora-welfare contingency plans.
prelimsPointers: The JCPOA was signed in 2015 between Iran and the P5+1 (China, France, Russia, UK, US plus Germany).
India operates the Chabahar port project in Iran, which provides sea-land access to Afghanistan and Central Asia bypassing Pakistan.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how renewed US–Iran confrontation in West Asia tests India's balancing act between energy security, diaspora interests and its partnership with the United States.

static.topic: UN Security Council and Conflict Governance in West Asia
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Global Governance and UN Reform
static.whatIsIt: The UN Security Council, with five permanent veto-wielding members and ten elected members serving two-year terms, holds primary responsibility for international peace and security. India has long sought permanent membership.
static.background: India is a founding UN member and among the largest troop contributors to UN peacekeeping. The G4 — India, Brazil, Germany and Japan — campaigns for Council expansion, while the Intergovernmental Negotiations process remains inconclusive and the African Ezulwini Consensus shapes the reform debate.
static.whyInNews: Escalation between the US and Iran in the Strait of Hormuz renews questions about the Security Council's capacity to act when a permanent member is itself a party to the conflict.
static.wayForward: India should press for text-based negotiations on UNSC reform and use its voice in the UN General Assembly to argue for restraint and de-escalation in West Asia.
prelimsPointers: The UNSC has 15 members: 5 permanent (China, France, Russia, UK, US) and 10 elected for two-year terms.
The International Court of Justice sits at The Hague; the UN headquarters is in New York.
static.mainsAngle: Assess whether the UNSC's veto structure undermines conflict resolution in West Asia, and evaluate the case for India's permanent membership.

stories.headline: Cyclone Murasu makes landfall in Andhra; heavy rain, 120 kmph winds
stories.summary: Cyclone Murasu made landfall along the Andhra Pradesh coast on November 3, 2026, as the second severe cyclonic storm in a week. The storm brought heavy rainfall and winds reaching up to 120 kmph, with its eye crossing the coast before weakening into a deep depression by Tuesday midnight, when wind speeds were expected to fall to around 75 kmph. Bapatla, Prakasam and Krishna districts reported uprooted trees, damaged homes and inundated crops. Trains and flights to and from Vijayawada were cancelled, and the IMD identified Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu as the worst-hit states. Karnataka announced it would deploy 500 trained workers to help restore power in Andhra Pradesh.
stories.whyItMatters: Cyclone Murasu is a current example of India's recurring east-coast cyclone vulnerability, useful for GS-I geography and GS-III disaster management questions on early warning, relief coordination and climate resilience.

static.topic: Tropical Cyclones and the Indian Monsoon
static.syllabusNode: Geography — Physical Geography of India
static.whatIsIt: Tropical cyclones are intense low-pressure systems over warm oceans, characterised by strong winds, heavy rain and storm surges; in India they form over the Bay of Bengal and Arabian Sea.
static.background: The Indian monsoon is a seasonal reversal of winds driven by differential heating, the ITCZ shift and the Tibetan Plateau's heat pump, delivering ~75% of annual rainfall during June–September. El Niño usually weakens the monsoon, La Niña strengthens it, and the Indian Ocean Dipole modulates it. Peninsular rivers are rain-fed, and the Western Ghats and Himalayan rivers define drainage.
static.geography: Bay of Bengal and Arabian Sea; coastal Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu and Odisha are cyclone-prone; the Eastern Ghats and coastal plains influence rainfall distribution.
static.socioEconomic: Cyclones cause loss of life, displacement, crop damage, power outages and transport disruption; coastal communities, farmers and fisherfolk are among the most vulnerable.
static.whyInNews: Cyclone Murasu made landfall along the Andhra Pradesh coast on November 3, 2026, bringing heavy rain and winds up to 120 kmph, and is expected to weaken into a deep depression.
static.wayForward: Strengthen early warning, cyclone shelters, mangrove buffers, and climate-resilient coastal infrastructure; integrate disaster risk reduction with local development planning.
prelimsPointers: Himalayan rivers are perennial (snow-fed); peninsular rivers are seasonal.
Western Ghats lie west of the Deccan; highest peak Anamudi (Kerala).
static.mainsAngle: Monsoon variability and climate change; disaster preparedness for floods/cyclones.

static.topic: Agriculture, MSP and Food Security
static.syllabusNode: Economy — Agriculture & Food Security
static.whatIsIt: Minimum Support Price (MSP) is announced by the government on CACP recommendations for 22 mandated crops; food security is backed by the National Food Security Act, 2013, and PM Garib Kalyan Anna Yojana grain distribution.
static.background: Green Revolution (1960s) made India food-sufficient. Shanta Kumar Committee (2015) reviewed FCI operations. PM-KISAN gives ₹6,000/year income support. The three 2020 farm laws were repealed in 2021.
static.socioEconomic: Crop inundation can affect farm incomes, food supply and rural livelihoods; relief and compensation mechanisms become critical after cyclones.
static.whyInNews: Cyclone Murasu inundated crops in Bapatla, Prakasam and Krishna districts, raising concerns for standing crops and farmer livelihoods.
static.wayForward: Link disaster relief with crop insurance, timely compensation, and resilient agricultural practices; strengthen procurement and food security buffers.
prelimsPointers: MSP is a price assurance, not a legal right; procurement is concentrated in wheat/paddy.
NFSA covers up to 75% rural and 50% urban population.
static.mainsAngle: Reforming MSP and procurement while raising farmer incomes; water-fertiliser sustainability.

stories.headline: US midterms: voters deliver verdict on Trump's second term
stories.summary: Americans are voting in the 2026 midterm elections, widely framed as a verdict on the first two years of President Donald Trump's second term, with control of Congress at stake. Forecast models, including Nate Silver's final FLIPR and The Conversation's analysis, show Democrats favoured to win the House and holding an 82% chance of taking the Senate, with late movement in their direction. On the eve of polling, the US Supreme Court rejected the Trump administration's bid to stop California counting disputed ballots, while markets turned cautious and gold eased. Campaign debate has centred on economic grievances, even as foreign policy is being treated as a local issue; the result will reshape US politics and carry spillovers for partners such as New Zealand and India.
stories.whyItMatters: US midterm outcomes can alter congressional checks on the White House, affecting trade, defence, technology and Indo-Pacific policy — all directly relevant to India's multi-alignment and strategic autonomy.

static.topic: Judicial review and election disputes: the Supreme Court's role

static.whatIsIt: The Supreme Court (Art. 124) is India's apex court and guardian of the Constitution; High Courts (Art. 214) are at the state level. Judicial review is the power to test laws and state actions against the Constitution.
static.background: The collegium system evolved through the Three Judges Cases (1981, 1993, 1998). Kesavananda Bharati (1973) established the basic-structure doctrine. PILs expanded access to justice from the late 1970s, and Articles 32 and 226 provide writ jurisdiction.

static.wayForward: Compare judicial review in electoral matters across democracies; in India, focus on judicial independence, timely disposal of election petitions and institutional credibility.

stories.headline: Delhi AQI hits 'very poor' as SC permits green crackers
stories.summary: The Supreme Court has permitted the bursting of certified green firecrackers in Delhi-NCR on November 7 and 8, with specified windows of 6–7 am and 8–10 pm, according to reports. The bench observed that while a blanket firecracker ban 'seems ideal', there is insufficient data to conclude that prohibition alone solves air pollution. Separately, Delhi's air quality deteriorated sharply: AQI rose from 117 on Saturday to 261 on Sunday, and by Monday's 4 pm bulletin it reached 324, crossing into 'very poor' for the first time this season. The developments place judicial regulation of festive emissions alongside the broader winter pollution crisis in the capital region.
stories.whyItMatters: The story links judicial review, environmental regulation and public health in Delhi-NCR, a recurring UPSC theme under GS-II judiciary and GS-III environment.

static.topic: Supreme Court, Judicial Review and Preventive Detention

static.whatIsIt: The Supreme Court (Article 124) is the apex court and guardian of the Constitution; judicial review is its power to test executive and legislative action against the Constitution. Preventive detention — detention without trial to prevent a future offence — is permitted by Article 22(4)–(7) but hedged with procedural safeguards.
static.background: The collegium system evolved through the Three Judges Cases (1981, 1993, 1998); Kesavananda Bharati (1973) established the basic-structure doctrine; PILs expanded access to justice from the late 1970s. Article 32 (Supreme Court) and Article 226 (High Courts) provide writ jurisdiction.
static.socioEconomic: Adverse judicial remarks against serving officials carry career and reputational consequences, and careless observations in detention matters can prejudice both personal liberty and service records.
static.whyInNews: The Supreme Court expunged adverse remarks against a Tamil Nadu IPS officer and stressed that courts must be careful while commenting in preventive-detention cases.
static.wayForward: Greater judicial discipline in recording observations, reasoned rather than casual remarks, and clearer standards for when and how adverse remarks against officials are expunged.

static.topic: Burden of proof in matrimonial deaths — Section 106, Evidence Act
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Judiciary / Criminal Justice
static.whatIsIt: Section 106 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 places the burden of proving a fact especially within a person's knowledge on that person. The Supreme Court applied it to hold that inmates of a matrimonial home must explain an unnatural death of a woman occurring there.
static.background: The Evidence Act, 1872 was a colonial codification; from 1 July 2024 it stands replaced by the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, part of the new criminal-law trio along with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita and the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita. In Shambhu Nath Mehra v. State of Ajmer (1956) the Supreme Court held that Section 106 cannot be used to relieve the prosecution of its primary burden; in Trimukh Maroti Kirkan v. State of Maharashtra (2006) the provision was applied to a death inside the matrimonial home.
static.socioEconomic: Unnatural deaths of women in matrimonial homes typically occur in private settings with few independent witnesses, making the allocation of the burden of proof central to whether such deaths are prosecuted or go unpunished.
static.whyInNews: The Supreme Court ruled that inmates of a matrimonial home must explain an unnatural death of a woman, invoking Section 106 of the Evidence Act.
static.wayForward: Strengthen investigation and forensic capacity, and lay down clear standards so that the Section 106 exception is not stretched into an inversion of the presumption of innocence.
prelimsPointers: Section 106 IEA: the burden of proving a fact especially within a person's knowledge lies on that person.
The Evidence Act, 1872 was replaced by the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, in force from 1 July 2024.
Shambhu Nath Mehra v. State of Ajmer (1956): Section 106 does not shift the prosecution's primary burden of proof.
static.mainsAngle: Is Section 106 of the Evidence Act a calibrated exception or a de facto reversal of the burden of proof? Examine with reference to unnatural deaths in matrimonial homes.

prelims: Section 106 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 (now carried into the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023): the burden of proving a fact especially within a person's knowledge lies on that person.

stories.headline: BJP, Congress Spar Over Ramlila Maidan Rally as SIR Protests Continue
stories.summary: Opposition parties, led by the Congress, rallied at Delhi's Ramlila Maidan against the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, with The Wire reporting large crowds and a sharply anti-incumbency mood directed at the Prime Minister. The Election Commission's revision drive continues even as the political row over its conduct and consequences escalates.

static.topic: Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of Electoral Rolls
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Elections, Electoral Reforms and the Election Commission
static.whatIsIt: SIR is an intensive, house-to-house revision of electoral rolls carried out by the Election Commission of India, in which booth-level officers verify the particulars of existing electors and enumerate eligible persons, with the stated aim of removing dead, shifted, duplicate or otherwise ineligible entries.
static.background: Electoral rolls are prepared and revised under the Representation of the People Act, 1950 and the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960, with superintendence, direction and control vested in the ECI by Article 324. Revision is ordinarily an annual exercise, but the ECI has used the 'special intensive' mode for a full re-verification of rolls in a state, relying on door-to-door enumeration. Such drives have repeatedly drawn objections from opposition parties and civil-society groups over large-scale deletions, documentation burdens and the risk of disenfranchising genuine voters.
static.geography: Conducted state-wise; recent drives have been concentrated in specific states, while the current protests are centred on Delhi's Ramlila Maidan.
static.socioEconomic: Documentation requirements can disproportionately burden migrants, informal-sector workers, women and the elderly, raising concerns about exclusion from the electoral roll and about the cost of repeated verification on poor households.
static.whyInNews: Opposition parties, led by the Congress, held a rally at Ramlila Maidan against SIR; the BJP and Congress have since clashed over the rally's size, an AI-generated photograph and its reported impact on Delhi's festive trade.
static.wayForward: Ensure transparent, publicly auditable deletion lists with reasoned orders, accessible appeal mechanisms before Electoral Registration Officers and the ECI, and proactive publication of revision statistics so that roll purification does not erode trust in the electoral process.
prelimsPointers: Article 324 vests the superintendence, direction and control of the preparation of electoral rolls in the Election Commission of India.
Electoral rolls are prepared under the Representation of the People Act, 1950 read with the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960.
A person is ordinarily eligible for registration as an elector on attaining 18 years of age on the qualifying date.
static.mainsAngle: Examine whether intensive roll-revision exercises strengthen electoral integrity or risk excluding legitimate voters; suggest procedural safeguards consistent with Article 324 and the constitutional right to vote.

static.topic: Right to Protest and Peaceful Assembly

static.whatIsIt: Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(b) guarantee freedom of speech and expression and the right to assemble peaceably and without arms, subject to reasonable restrictions under Articles 19(2) and 19(3) in the interests of public order, sovereignty and integrity of India.
static.background: Ramlila Maidan in Delhi has been a recurring venue for mass political mobilisation, including the 2011 anti-corruption agitation. The Supreme Court has repeatedly held that the right to peaceful protest is a fundamental right and that restrictions on it must be reasonable, proportionate and imposed through lawful procedure rather than administrative discretion.
static.geography: Ramlila Maidan, central Delhi — a large open ground historically used for public meetings, agitations and political rallies.
static.socioEconomic: Mass rallies impose costs on surrounding traders and residents, and policing and permission arrangements frequently become a political flashpoint between rival parties.
static.whyInNews: The Congress-led rally against SIR at Ramlila Maidan, and the subsequent BJP–Congress dispute over crowd claims and reported losses to festive-season businesses, has put the regulation and politics of public protest in focus.
static.wayForward: Codify transparent, non-discriminatory conditions for permission to protest, with time-bound reasoned orders and proportionate policing, so that assembly rights are not curtailed by administrative discretion.
prelimsPointers: Article 19(1)(b) guarantees the right to assemble peaceably and without arms; Article 19(3) permits reasonable restrictions in the interests of public order.
The right to protest is not absolute and is subject to reasonable restrictions upheld by the Supreme Court.
Ramlila Maidan in Delhi is a well-known venue for mass public meetings and agitations.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how the balance between the right to peaceful assembly and the state's duty to maintain public order should be struck in an era of large-scale political mobilisation.

stories.headline: India's Scotch import probe rattles liquor majors amid UK trade pact rollout
stories.summary: India's trade remedies authority has opened an investigation into imports of Scotch whisky from the United Kingdom, a move that has unsettled global liquor majors for whom India is one of the fastest-growing premium spirits markets. The probe, which could lead to provisional duties on Scotch, follows complaints from domestic producers and sits awkwardly with the tariff concessions New Delhi extended to London under their recently signed bilateral trade agreement. Government sources indicate that New Delhi is simultaneously working to resolve the tariff dispute within the framework of that agreement, suggesting the investigation may function as negotiating leverage rather than a permanent barrier. The episode illustrates the recurring tension between India's use of WTO-permitted trade remedies and the market-access commitments it undertakes in free trade agreements.

static.topic: India–UK Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA)
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Bilateral Agreements; India & the World
static.whatIsIt: A comprehensive free trade agreement between India and the United Kingdom covering goods, services, investment, intellectual property and rules of origin, with dedicated chapters on mobility and digital trade.
static.background: Negotiations were launched in 2022 and the agreement was signed in 2025; it now awaits completion of ratification and implementation formalities on both sides. In the goods package, India agreed to steep cuts in duties on Scotch whisky and UK gin, with the whisky tariff scheduled to fall in stages over roughly a decade. Alcohol remains politically sensitive in India because states, not the Centre, levy excise on it.
static.geography: United Kingdom; the UK is among India's largest trading partners in Europe, while India is a priority growth market for UK distillers.
static.socioEconomic: The pact is expected to boost Indian textiles, leather, gems and jewellery and marine exports, and to ease mobility for professionals and students; the alcohol tariff schedule was the most contested element of the goods negotiations.
static.whyInNews: A trade remedies investigation into Scotch imports coincides with efforts to implement the tariff commitments made under the UK trade pact.
static.wayForward: Early ratification and implementation; aligning trade remedy actions with FTA commitments; addressing state-level excise and licensing barriers that limit actual market access.

static.topic: Trade Remedies in India: Anti-Dumping and Safeguard Measures
static.syllabusNode: Economy — External Sector; Trade Policy and Protectionism
static.whatIsIt: WTO-permitted contingent protection measures: anti-dumping duty against imports sold below normal value, countervailing duty against subsidised imports, and safeguard duty against a sudden surge in imports causing serious injury.
static.background: These measures derive from GATT Article VI and the WTO Anti-Dumping Agreement, the SCM Agreement and the Safeguards Agreement. In India, the Directorate General of Trade Remedies (DGTR), under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, conducts investigations and recommends duties; the Ministry of Finance imposes them. Measures are subject to sunset reviews and can be challenged at the WTO.
static.socioEconomic: Domestic producers seek protection from cheap imports, while user industries and consumers bear higher prices; frequent use of remedies can invite retaliation or dispute settlement by trading partners.
static.whyInNews: The investigation into Scotch whisky imports from the UK is the immediate trigger for the current controversy.
static.wayForward: Time-bound, transparent investigations; ensuring measures are WTO-consistent and do not undercut commitments made under bilateral trade agreements.
prelimsPointers: DGTR recommends trade remedy duties; the Ministry of Finance imposes them.
Anti-dumping duties are country- and product-specific, whereas safeguard duties are applied on a non-discriminatory basis.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss whether trade remedy measures are increasingly being used as instruments of protectionism and what this implies for India's FTA strategy.

static.topic: WTO and the Rules-Based Multilateral Trading System
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Global Governance and Multilateralism
static.whatIsIt: The World Trade Organization, established in 1995 as successor to GATT (1947), administers multilateral trade rules, hosts negotiations and settles disputes through its Dispute Settlement Body.
static.background: GATT 1947 was replaced by the Marrakesh Agreement (1994), bringing the WTO into being on 1 January 1995. The Appellate Body has been paralysed since 2019 because members have not been appointed, prompting some countries to use the Multi-Party Interim Appeal Arbitration Arrangement (MPIA).
static.socioEconomic: A functioning dispute settlement system gives smaller economies predictability; its paralysis encourages unilateral tariffs and retaliatory measures.
static.whyInNews: Trade remedy actions and tariff disputes of the kind at issue must be consistent with WTO obligations, and the episode illustrates the strain on the multilateral system.
static.wayForward: Reform and revive the dispute settlement mechanism, restore the Appellate Body, and safeguard special and differential treatment for developing members.
prelimsPointers: The WTO was established on 1 January 1995 and is headquartered in Geneva.
The Appellate Body has been non-functional since 2019 due to vacancies.
static.mainsAngle: Assess the implications of the crisis in WTO dispute settlement for developing countries that rely on rules-based trade remedies.

prelims: Trade remedy investigations in India are conducted by the Directorate General of Trade Remedies (DGTR) under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry; the duty is imposed by the Ministry of Finance.
Anti-dumping duties target a product from a specific country, while safeguard duties address a surge in imports irrespective of source.
Taxation and regulation of alcoholic beverages is largely a State subject — excise on alcoholic liquors for human consumption is Entry 51 of the State List.
The India–UK trade agreement signed in 2025 provides for a staged reduction of tariffs on Scotch whisky and UK gin.

stories.headline: Discom payment safeguards key to India's renewable energy targets
stories.summary: India's renewable capacity build-out rests on power purchase agreements between generators and electricity distribution companies, and those contracts are only as reliable as a discom's ability to pay on time. ThePrint examines the weaknesses in the payment-security architecture meant to shield generators from delayed receivables, arguing that a PPA is only as good as the discom's payment capacity. In parallel, industry voices at the Bharat RE summit argue that global partnerships can help Indian solar manufacturers scale up and export. Taken together, the two strands point to a financing-and-manufacturing bottleneck sitting between India's headline renewable targets and their actual delivery.
stories.whyItMatters: It ties the financial health of the power distribution sector directly to India's climate and energy-transition commitments — a recurring GS-III theme spanning infrastructure financing, discom reform and renewable energy. It also links domestic manufacturing capacity to India's external economic partnerships.

static.topic: Discom finances and payment security for power generators
static.syllabusNode: Infrastructure — Energy; Power sector reforms
static.whatIsIt: Distribution companies buy electricity from generators under long-term power purchase agreements and sell it to consumers at regulated tariffs. Payment security mechanisms — letters of credit, escrow arrangements, payment security funds and late payment surcharges — are designed to ensure generators are paid on schedule.
static.background: The Electricity Act, 2003 unbundled generation, transmission and distribution and created a regulatory architecture for tariffs and open access. Persistent financial stress in discoms led to UDAY (Ujwal DISCOM Assurance Yojana), launched by the Ministry of Power in 2015, which took over a share of discom debt and pushed operational improvements. The Ministry of Power later notified Late Payment Surcharge Rules in 2022 to give generators a statutory route to recover overdue dues.
static.geography: Discom health varies sharply across states, and the resource-rich renewable states depend on transmission evacuation to load centres.
static.socioEconomic: Tariff subsidies, commitments to free or subsidised agricultural power, and aggregate technical and commercial losses shape discom cash flows; payment delays ultimately raise the cost of capital for renewable developers and are passed through to consumers.
static.whyInNews: Renewable payment safeguards are under scrutiny as delayed discom payments threaten the bankability of power purchase agreements and, by extension, fresh renewable capacity addition.
static.wayForward: Enforce payment security and late-payment rules, shift subsidy delivery to direct benefit transfer, reduce AT&C losses, and align tariffs with the cost of supply so that PPAs remain bankable.
prelimsPointers: UDAY was launched in 2015 by the Ministry of Power to restructure discom debt and improve operational efficiency.
The Electricity Act, 2003 is the principal law governing generation, transmission, distribution and trading of electricity.

static.topic: India's renewable energy targets and climate commitments

static.whatIsIt: India's non-fossil generating capacity target of 500 GW by 2030, announced as part of the Panchamrit commitments at COP26 in Glasgow, alongside a net zero pledge for 2070.
static.background: India's renewable push began with the Electricity Act, 2003 and the National Action Plan on Climate Change (2008), under which the National Solar Mission was launched in 2010. Competitive bidding drove solar tariffs down sharply and capacity has grown rapidly since.
static.geography: Solar and wind capacity is concentrated in Gujarat, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh; evacuation of power from these resource-rich states to demand centres is a binding constraint.
static.socioEconomic: Land acquisition, rooftop adoption, and employment in manufacturing and installation are key socio-economic dimensions of the transition.
static.whyInNews: Payment delays to generators and gaps in domestic manufacturing are cited as risks to meeting the 2030 non-fossil capacity target.
static.wayForward: Strengthen transmission evacuation, expand domestic manufacturing, and lock in payment security so that developers can raise finance at reasonable cost.

stories.headline: CDSCO widens drug import gateways, mandates digital batchwise clearance for high-risk solvents
stories.summary: The Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare has proposed expanding the list of authorised import gateways through which drugs, medical devices and cosmetics may enter India, a move aimed at reducing port-level bottlenecks and widening market access. static.topic: Drug Regulation in India: CDSCO, Import Gateways and the Drugs and Cosmetics Act
static.syllabusNode: Governance — Government Policies and Interventions; Health
static.whatIsIt: India's drug, medical device and cosmetics regulation is anchored in the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 and the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945, administered by the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) under the Directorate General of Health Services, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. The Drugs Controller General of India (DCGI) heads CDSCO. Imports of drugs and cosmetics are permitted only through notified ports/gateways, and the proposal to expand this list is the core of the current news.
static.background: The Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 created a dual Centre–State regulatory structure: the Centre handles approvals, imports, and standards, while States license manufacturing and sale. Medical devices were brought under a dedicated Medical Devices Rules, 2017 framework, and cosmetics under the Cosmetics Rules, 2020. Over time, CDSCO has moved from paper-based to online licensing and clearance through its digital portals, with batchwise tracking of high-risk inputs being the latest step.
static.geography: Import gateways are notified ports and airports; expansion changes the geography of entry for pharmaceutical consignments into India.
static.socioEconomic: Affects availability and cost of medicines and devices, the compliance burden on importers and small traders, and the competitiveness of India's pharmaceutical sector.
static.whyInNews: The Health Ministry has proposed widening the authorised import gateways for drugs, medical devices and cosmetics, while CDSCO has mandated digital batchwise clearance for high-risk pharmaceutical solvents.
static.wayForward: Pair gateway expansion with uniform, digitally auditable clearance standards across all notified ports, and build testing and post-import surveillance capacity so that facilitation does not dilute quality assurance.
prelimsPointers: CDSCO functions under the Directorate General of Health Services, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, and is headed by the DCGI.
Drugs and cosmetics may be imported into India only through notified ports/gateways.

static.mainsAngle: Examine how regulatory reform in drug import clearance balances trade facilitation against quality and health-security safeguards.

static.topic: Digital Public Infrastructure and Data Governance in Regulatory Clearance
static.syllabusNode: Governance — e-Governance, Transparency and Accountability
static.whatIsIt: India's Digital Public Infrastructure — Aadhaar, UPI and DigiLocker — is a layered, interoperable stack on which sectoral regulators build digital workflows. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 governs processing of personal data, creating a Data Protection Board and a consent-based framework. CDSCO's move to digital batchwise clearance is an instance of regulatory workflow digitisation.
static.background: Aadhaar (UIDAI, 2009) is the world's largest biometric ID system; UPI (NPCI, 2016) processes billions of monthly transactions. The DPDP Act introduced consent-based processing, data-principal rights and obligations for significant data fiduciaries. Regulators across sectors have progressively shifted licensing, returns and clearances onto digital portals.
static.socioEconomic: Digitised clearance reduces physical touchpoints and discretion, but requires importers — including smaller firms — to have the digital capacity to comply with batchwise reporting.
static.whyInNews: CDSCO's mandate of digital batchwise clearance for high-risk pharmaceutical solvents is a regulatory application of India's broader digital governance architecture.
static.wayForward: Ensure interoperability of regulatory portals with trade and customs systems, provide onboarding support for small importers, and align data handling with the DPDP Act's consent and purpose-limitation principles.
prelimsPointers: NPCI operates UPI, RuPay, IMPS and NACH.
The DPDP Act, 2023 provides for consent-based processing, data-principal rights and significant data fiduciaries.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how digitising regulatory clearances can improve transparency while raising questions of data protection and digital capacity for smaller enterprises.

static.topic: Pharmaceutical Supply-Chain Security and Strategic Autonomy
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — India and the World; Economy — Industrial Policy
static.whatIsIt: India is a major global supplier of generic formulations but depends substantially on imported bulk drugs and intermediates, particularly from a single dominant source country. Supply-chain security for active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) is therefore treated as both an economic and a strategic-autonomy concern.
static.background: India's foreign policy framework combines strategic autonomy and multi-alignment, engaging simultaneously with the Quad, BRICS, SCO, G20 and IBSA — a posture rooted in NAM (1961) and Panchsheel (1954) and reshaped after the 1991 liberalisation and the 1998 nuclear tests. In the economic domain, this autonomy logic has translated into incentives for domestic manufacturing of critical inputs, including Production Linked Incentive schemes for bulk drugs and pharmaceuticals.
static.geography: Import dependence concentrates sourcing in specific supplier geographies, making the supply chain vulnerable to disruption at source and at Indian ports of entry.
static.socioEconomic: Input security affects medicine prices, availability and the viability of India's domestic formulation industry and its export competitiveness.
static.whyInNews: Changes to import gateways and batchwise clearance for high-risk solvents directly affect the flow of critical pharmaceutical inputs into India.
static.wayForward: Diversify sourcing of APIs and intermediates, scale domestic bulk-drug capacity, and maintain buffer stocks of critical inputs alongside streamlined but rigorous import clearance.
prelimsPointers: India assumed the G20 presidency in 2022–23; the African Union was admitted as a permanent G20 member in 2023.
India and Pakistan joined the SCO in 2017.
static.mainsAngle: Analyse how India's dependence on imported pharmaceutical inputs shapes its industrial policy and its pursuit of strategic autonomy.

prelims: CDSCO, headed by the DCGI, is India's national drug regulator under the Directorate General of Health Services, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare.
Drugs, medical devices and cosmetics may be imported into India only through notified authorised import gateways/ports.
CDSCO has mandated digital batchwise clearance for high-risk pharmaceutical solvents, tightening consignment-level verification.
The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 provides the consent-based framework governing digital processing of personal data in such regulatory systems.
stories.mainsQuestion: The expansion of authorised drug import gateways alongside mandatory digital batchwise clearance reflects a wider shift in India's regulatory governance. Examine how such reforms balance trade facilitation, quality assurance and data-governance concerns.

stories.headline: Pro-Kannada outfit campaigns for local jobs in Bengaluru IT-BT firms
stories.summary: A pro-Kannada outfit has launched a campaign demanding preferential employment of Kannadigas in Bengaluru's IT and biotechnology (BT) firms. Deccan Herald reports the launch of the campaign aimed at 'protecting' jobs for local candidates in the IT-BT sector, while The News Minute reports that members of the group have begun visiting company offices in the city to press the demand. The mobilisation taps a long-running 'son-of-the-soil' sentiment in Karnataka, where local-hiring assertions surface periodically against the backdrop of large-scale migration into Bengaluru's knowledge economy. The demand sits awkwardly with the industry's reliance on merit-based, pan-India recruitment and with constitutional protections on equality of opportunity in employment and freedom to practise any trade or profession. No legislative or administrative action by the state government has been reported in these accounts.
stories.whyItMatters: The episode revives the debate on local-hiring quotas in private industry — a live GS-III employment issue with GS-II and GS-I overlaps on equality, federalism and linguistic regionalism. It is a useful case for questions on labour mobility, affirmative action beyond the state, and the politics of migration in India's metropolitan growth hubs.

perspectives.take: Frames the development primarily as a campaign 'to protect jobs for Kannadigas' in IT-BT firms, foregrounding the local-jobs grievance and the launch of the mobilisation.

Focuses on the campaign's methods — group members visiting IT company offices in Bengaluru — framing it as an active, on-the-ground push for more jobs for Kannadigas; a strong regional/state-focused lens.

static.topic: Poverty, Inequality & Employment — local hiring quotas in private industry
static.syllabusNode: Economy — Inclusive Growth & Employment; also GS-II (Governance, Rights)
static.whatIsIt: The demand that private firms give preference to local residents ('sons of the soil') is a form of sub-national affirmative action. Unlike reservations in public employment, there is no general constitutional mandate for private-sector local quotas; such preferences would have to be legislated and would face scrutiny under equality and trade-freedom guarantees.
static.background: Employment data in India is tracked through the Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS), launched in 2017, which reports quarterly urban and annual all-India estimates. Poverty is tracked through consumption surveys and NITI Aayog's National Multidimensional Poverty Index (2021), which uses 12 indicators across health, education and living standards. States have periodically attempted local-hiring laws for private industry; implementation has been contested and contested in courts or left un-notified, and industry bodies have opposed mandatory local quotas on grounds of skills availability and mobility.
static.geography: Bengaluru is India's largest IT-BT cluster and a magnet for inter-state migration, which is the immediate backdrop to local-hiring demands.
static.socioEconomic: Ties to the quality-of-employment question: a large informal sector, skills mismatch and regional imbalances in job creation push local populations to demand protected access to the formal, high-wage knowledge sector.
static.whyInNews: A pro-Kannada outfit has launched a campaign and is visiting IT-BT company offices in Bengaluru to demand more jobs for Kannadigas.
static.wayForward: Policy attention is better directed at skilling local youth for the knowledge economy, transparently mapping skill gaps with industry, and enforcing existing labour protections — rather than quotas that risk restricting mobility and inviting legal challenge.
keyTerms: Article 16 (equality of opportunity in public employment)
prelimsPointers: NITI Aayog's National MPI covers 3 dimensions (health, education, standard of living) and 12 indicators.
Unemployment Rate = unemployed persons / labour force; PLFS reports both urban quarterly and all-India annual estimates.
Article 16(3) permits Parliament alone to prescribe residence as a qualification for employment under a State government or local authority — it does not cover private employment.
static.mainsAngle: Quality of employment, structural transformation and the skills gap — examine whether local-hiring mandates address the underlying problem of inadequate job creation.

static.topic: Linguistic identity, regionalism and state formation
static.syllabusNode: Society — Diversity of India; Regionalism & Linguistic Identity (also GS-II Federalism)
static.whatIsIt: Linguistic identity has been a central organising principle of Indian statehood since the States Reorganisation Act, 1956, which redrew boundaries largely along language lines. In Karnataka, this identity is asserted through the Kannada language movement and the marking of Karnataka Rajyotsava.
static.background: Karnataka was constituted on 1 November 1956 as Mysore State under the States Reorganisation Act, 1956, and was renamed Karnataka in 1973. Kannada was a major focus of the state's linguistic consolidation, and periodic mobilisations — over language in education, signage and employment — have recurred since. Kannada was accorded the status of a classical language by the Centre.
static.geography: Karnataka, with Bengaluru as its capital and principal global-services hub; the state shares borders with Maharashtra, Goa, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu and Kerala, all with their own linguistic assertions.
static.socioEconomic: Rapid, high-skill in-migration into Bengaluru raises anxieties about cultural visibility and access to jobs among local residents, fuelling identity-based mobilisation.
static.whyInNews: The current campaign invokes Karnataka's linguistic identity in the domain of private-sector employment.
static.wayForward: Accommodating linguistic identity in public services, education and cultural policy while preserving constitutional guarantees of equality and free movement avoids converting cultural assertion into exclusion.
keyTerms: Article 29 (protection of cultural and educational rights of minorities)
Article 19(1)(g) (freedom to practise any profession or trade)
prelimsPointers: Karnataka was formed on 1 November 1956 as Mysore State and renamed Karnataka in 1973; Rajyotsava is observed on 1 November.
The States Reorganisation Act, 1956 reorganised states largely along linguistic lines.
static.mainsAngle: Linguistic sub-nationalism can strengthen cultural federalism even as it risks exclusionary politics — assess with reference to metropolitan migration.

static.topic: Inter-state migration, labour mobility and Indian federalism
static.syllabusNode: Society — Population & Associated Issues; GS-II — Federalism
static.whatIsIt: India's Constitution guarantees citizens the right to move freely throughout the territory of India and to reside and settle in any part of it, which underpins large-scale internal migration from less-industrialised states to employment hubs.
static.background: Internal migration in India is overwhelmingly inter-state and directed at urban agglomerations. Post-liberalisation growth concentrated IT, IT-enabled services and manufacturing in cities such as Bengaluru, Pune, Hyderabad and the National Capital Region, drawing workers from across the country and creating tensions over housing, infrastructure and perceived competition for jobs.
static.geography: Bengaluru's service-sector-led growth has made it a national destination for skilled migrants, particularly from Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and northern states.
static.socioEconomic: Migration raises productivity and remittance flows for sending regions while creating localised pressures on public services and identity politics in receiving regions.
static.whyInNews: The pro-Kannada campaign for local hiring is a receiving-region reaction to sustained in-migration for IT-BT jobs.
static.wayForward: Balanced regional development, investment in tier-2 and tier-3 cities, portable social-security benefits for migrants and credible local skilling pathways together reduce the friction that nativist demands feed on.
prelimsPointers: Articles 19(1)(d) and 19(1)(e) guarantee freedom of movement and of residence and settlement throughout India, subject to reasonable restrictions.
Census-based migration data is complemented by the PLFS, which captures migration and labour-market characteristics.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how intra-national labour mobility interacts with identity politics in India's growth centres, and suggest institutional responses.

prelims: A pro-Kannada outfit has launched a campaign seeking greater employment of Kannadigas in Bengaluru's IT and biotechnology (BT) firms, with members visiting company offices to press the demand (reported November 2026).
Bengaluru is India's principal IT-BT cluster and a major destination for inter-state skilled migration.

Article 16(3) of the Constitution allows only Parliament — not State legislatures — to prescribe residence as a qualification for employment under a State government or local authority; private-sector employment is not covered.
Articles 19(1)(d) and 19(1)(e) guarantee citizens the right to move freely and to reside and settle anywhere in India.
stories.mainsQuestion: Demands for preferential employment of local residents in private industry are increasingly voiced in India's metropolitan growth hubs. Examine the constitutional and economic implications of such local-hiring quotas, and suggest alternative policy responses that reconcile local aspirations with the right to mobility.

stories.headline: Delhi Police ACP suspended after personnel protest at headquarters
stories.summary: An Assistant Commissioner of Police in the Delhi Police was suspended after personnel gathered in protest at the force's headquarters, an unusual instance of open dissent by uniformed staff. Reports identify the officer as Manasvi Vashishta, described as having led the gathering. The episode has shifted attention from the individual disciplinary action to the wider question of how grievances inside the force are handled, with commentary arguing that the protest reflects a weak internal redress mechanism rather than an isolated lapse. Delhi Police, unlike State police forces, is administered by the Union Ministry of Home Affairs, a consequence of the capital's special constitutional arrangement.
stories.whyItMatters: It links a live disciplinary episode to the static themes of police reform, internal accountability and Delhi's asymmetric federal setup — recurring areas for governance and federalism questions.

perspectives.take: Frames the episode as evidence of a failing internal grievance system, treating the problem as structural rather than individual — an opinion/editorial framing.
Reports the suspension as straight news and profiles the officer who led the protest, focusing on the event and the individual rather than systemic causes.

static.topic: Police reforms in India
static.syllabusNode: Government Policies & Interventions; Role of Civil Services; Internal Security — Police Reforms
static.whatIsIt: A long-pending agenda to make Indian police forces more accountable, professional and insulated from undue external control, covering recruitment, tenure security, oversight bodies and internal grievance redress.
static.background: Police is a State subject under Entry 2 of the State List. Reform demands were crystallised by the National Police Commission and later by the Supreme Court's directives in Prakash Singh v. Union of India (2006), which mandated a State Security Commission, a minimum two-year tenure for the DGP, separation of investigation from law and order, a Police Establishment Board, a Police Complaints Authority and a National Security Commission. The Model Police Act, 2006 and the Second Administrative Reforms Commission's report on Ethics in Governance (2007) built on these ideas; implementation across States has been uneven.
static.socioEconomic: Working conditions, vacancies, long duty hours and limited avenues for internal grievance redress are recurring concerns; India's police-population ratio is widely noted to be below the UN-recommended benchmark.
static.whyInNews: The suspension of a Delhi Police ACP after personnel protested at the police headquarters has revived questions about discipline, morale and internal grievance mechanisms.
static.wayForward: Give statutory backing to the Supreme Court's directives, make Police Establishment Boards and Complaints Authorities functional, create independent grievance channels, and enforce predictable tenure and transfer norms.
keyTerms: Prakash Singh v. Union of India (2006)
prelimsPointers: Police and public order are State List subjects (Entries 1 and 2).
Prakash Singh (2006) laid down a set of directives on police reform.
The Model Police Act, 2006 was circulated to States for adoption.
static.mainsAngle: Examine why police reform directives have been unevenly implemented and how stronger internal grievance redress can improve accountability without undermining discipline.

static.topic: Delhi's special status and policing in the capital
static.syllabusNode: Federalism; Union Territories; Article 239AA
static.whatIsIt: Delhi is a Union Territory with a legislature whose powers exclude police, public order and land, which remain with the Union government.
static.background: The 69th Constitutional Amendment (1991) inserted Article 239AA, creating a Legislative Assembly for Delhi. Police, public order and land were kept out of its legislative competence. The Delhi Police is governed by the Delhi Police Act, 1978 and administered by the Ministry of Home Affairs through the Lieutenant Governor. Disputes over the division of Delhi's administrative powers have repeatedly reached the Supreme Court.
static.geography: Delhi, the National Capital Territory, is a Union Territory bordered by Haryana and Uttar Pradesh.
static.whyInNews: The protest and suspension at Delhi Police headquarters spotlight the force's direct line of accountability to the Centre rather than to the elected Delhi government.
static.wayForward: Clearer institutional protocols for internal discipline and grievance handling, alongside continued judicial clarification of the Centre–Delhi division of functions.
prelimsPointers: Article 239AA was inserted by the 69th Amendment Act, 1991.
Police, public order and land are outside the Delhi Assembly's legislative competence.
Delhi Police is administered by the Union Ministry of Home Affairs.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how Delhi's asymmetric federal arrangement affects accountability and service delivery in the capital.

static.topic: Grievance redressal in public institutions
static.syllabusNode: Governance; Citizen's Charter; Transparency & Accountability
static.whatIsIt: The institutional mechanisms through which public servants and citizens can seek redress of service-related grievances.
static.background: The Second Administrative Reforms Commission emphasised citizen-centric administration and effective grievance redress. CPGRAMS is the Centre's centralised online grievance platform, and several States and departments run their own internal channels. In uniformed services, grievances are typically routed through the chain of command, which critics say discourages escalated or collective complaints.
static.socioEconomic: Weak internal redress is associated with low morale, absenteeism and, in some cases, informal collective action by public servants.
static.whyInNews: Commentary on the Delhi Police episode argues that the protest signals a failing internal grievance system.
static.wayForward: Independent, time-bound grievance committees, protection against victimisation for complainants, and periodic morale and workplace audits.
prelimsPointers: CPGRAMS is the Government of India's centralised public grievance redress platform.
The Second ARC's fourth report, 'Ethics in Governance' (2007), dealt with grievance redress and police reform.
static.mainsAngle: How far do internal grievance mechanisms in uniformed services meet the principles of natural justice and accountability?

prelims: Delhi Police is a Union-administered force under the Ministry of Home Affairs, not under the elected Delhi government.
Police and public order are State List entries; for Delhi they fall outside the Assembly's competence under Article 239AA.
Prakash Singh v. Union of India (2006) is the key Supreme Court judgment on police reform.
CPGRAMS is the Centre's centralised public grievance redress platform.
stories.mainsQuestion: The protest by Delhi Police personnel and the subsequent suspension of an officer raise questions about discipline and internal grievance redress in uniformed services. Examine the structural weaknesses in India's police grievance mechanisms and suggest reforms consistent with the Supreme Court's directions in Prakash Singh (2006).

stories.headline: Supreme Court seeks Allahabad High Court reply on POCSO judge removal plea
stories.summary: The Supreme Court has sought a response from the Allahabad High Court on a plea seeking the removal of a judge who presides over POCSO matters and is facing a rape accusation. The order keeps the matter alive before the top court while inviting the High Court’s position on the prayer. The case raises questions about how allegations against a judicial officer are handled, especially where the judge’s docket involves sensitive child-protection cases. It also touches on the balance between judicial independence and accountability in the subordinate judiciary.
stories.whyItMatters: Directly relevant to GS-II judiciary: judicial accountability, High Court control over subordinate courts, and fair process in sensitive POCSO proceedings.

perspectives.take: Frames the development as the Supreme Court seeking the Allahabad High Court’s response on a plea to remove a POCSO judge facing a rape case, with a procedural legal-news focus.

static.topic: Supreme Court, High Courts & Judicial Review
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Judiciary
static.whatIsIt: The Supreme Court (Article 124) is the apex court and guardian of the Constitution; High Courts (Article 214) are at the state level. Judicial review is the power to test laws and executive action against the Constitution.
static.background: The collegium system evolved through the Three Judges Cases (1981, 1993, 1998). Kesavananda Bharati (1973) established the basic-structure doctrine. PILs expanded access to justice from the late 1970s. Articles 32 and 226 provide writ jurisdiction.
static.whyInNews: The Supreme Court has sought the Allahabad High Court’s response on a plea to remove a POCSO judge facing a rape accusation, highlighting questions of judicial accountability and institutional process.
static.wayForward: The High Court’s response and any ensuing inquiry should follow fair procedure, protect the complainant and witnesses, and maintain public confidence without undermining judicial independence.
prelimsPointers: Original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court covers disputes between the Centre and states under Article 131.
Advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court is under Article 143.
High Courts are constitutional courts established under Article 214.
static.mainsAngle: Examine judicial backlog, vacancies and pendency; the balance between judicial independence and accountability.

stories.mainsQuestion: Judicial independence and judicial accountability are often viewed as competing values. In the context of allegations against judicial officers, examine the constitutional and institutional mechanisms available to address misconduct while ensuring a fair process.

stories.headline: Indian Navy rescues hijacked fishing vessel off Somalia, frees 20 crew
stories.summary: The Indian Navy intercepted and rescued a hijacked fishing vessel off the coast of Somalia, securing the release of all 20 crew members on board. The operation, carried out with close coordination between the Navy and the Indian Air Force, involved locating and boarding the vessel after it had been seized by hijackers. Officials framed the mission as evidence of the Navy's operational preparedness and its capacity to execute complex maritime security tasks at extended ranges from the Indian coast. The rescue comes amid persistent concerns over piracy and armed robbery at sea in the Western Indian Ocean and the Gulf of Aden approaches, a corridor vital to India's trade and energy supplies.
stories.whyItMatters: Anti-piracy operations in the Western Indian Ocean sit at the intersection of India's maritime security doctrine, Indian Ocean Region diplomacy and the protection of sea lines of communication — a recurring theme in GS-II and GS-III questions on India's extended neighbourhood and internal security.

perspectives.take: Frames the rescue as a demonstration of the Navy's operational reach and Navy–Air Force jointness in complex maritime missions; a mainstream national-security framing with no critical angle on the operation.

static.topic: Maritime Piracy and India's Anti-Piracy Operations
static.syllabusNode: Internal Security — Security challenges and their management in border areas; role of external state and non-state actors
static.whatIsIt: Piracy is the commission of illegal acts of violence, detention or depredation for private ends by the crew or passengers of a private ship against another ship on the high seas. India's response combines naval deployments, air surveillance, information-sharing and multilateral frameworks.
static.background: Somali piracy surged between roughly 2008 and 2012, disrupting the Gulf of Aden and Western Indian Ocean shipping lanes, before declining after coordinated international naval patrols, shipboard hardening measures and armed guards. The Indian Navy began anti-piracy patrols in the Gulf of Aden in 2008 and has since conducted escort and interdiction missions, including Operation Sankalp launched in 2019 for maritime security in the Gulf of Oman and Persian Gulf. India participates in information-sharing arrangements such as the Information Fusion Centre – Indian Ocean Region (IFC-IOR), established in 2018 at Gurugram.
static.geography: The Gulf of Aden, Bab-el-Mandeb strait and the Western Indian Ocean off Somalia form a chokepoint corridor carrying a large share of India's westward trade and energy imports; the Somali coast's proximity to these lanes makes it a persistent piracy risk zone.
static.socioEconomic: Piracy raises insurance and freight costs, endangers Indian seafarers and fishermen, and can disrupt supply chains; coastal economies in the region depend heavily on fishing and shipping.
static.whyInNews: The Indian Navy, with Indian Air Force coordination, rescued a hijacked fishing vessel off Somalia and freed all 20 crew members.
static.wayForward: Sustained naval presence and aerial surveillance, deeper regional coordination with littoral states and multilateral task forces, stronger information-sharing through IFC-IOR, and adherence to international legal frameworks for prosecution of suspected pirates.
prelimsPointers: UNCLOS Article 100 obliges states to cooperate to the fullest possible extent in the repression of piracy on the high seas; Article 101 defines piracy.
The Djibouti Code of Conduct (2009) is a regional instrument for repressing piracy and armed robbery against ships in the Western Indian Ocean and Gulf of Aden.
Combined Task Force 151 is a multinational counter-piracy naval task force under the Combined Maritime Forces, headquartered in Bahrain.
static.mainsAngle: Evaluate the effectiveness of India's anti-piracy strategy in the Western Indian Ocean. How can naval diplomacy and regional institutions be leveraged to secure sea lines of communication?

static.topic: UNCLOS and Freedom of Navigation
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Important International institutions, agencies and fora, their structure and mandate
static.whatIsIt: The United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), adopted in 1982 and in force since 1994, is the framework treaty governing maritime zones, navigation rights, resource rights and obligations including suppression of piracy. India is a party.
static.background: UNCLOS codified the territorial sea (up to 12 nautical miles), contiguous zone, exclusive economic zone (up to 200 nautical miles) and continental shelf, and created institutions such as the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea (ITLOS) and the International Seabed Authority. It also preserves the freedom of the high seas, including navigation and overflight.
static.geography: The high seas beyond national jurisdiction are where piracy enforcement powers, including hot pursuit and seizure, are exercised under UNCLOS and customary law.
static.socioEconomic: Maritime trade carries the bulk of global merchandise; legal certainty over navigation underpins shipping, insurance and port economies.
static.whyInNews: The rescue of a hijacked vessel on the high seas off Somalia illustrates the enforcement of UNCLOS-based anti-piracy obligations by a naval force.
static.wayForward: Strengthen universal adherence to UNCLOS, build capacity of littoral states for prosecution and maritime domain awareness, and support IMO-led measures for seafarer safety.
prelimsPointers: UNCLOS was adopted in 1982 and entered into force in 1994; India is a state party.
ITLOS is based in Hamburg, Germany; the International Seabed Authority is based in Kingston, Jamaica.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how UNCLOS balances freedom of navigation with the enforcement obligations of states in combating piracy and other threats at sea.

prelims: UNCLOS Article 100 requires all states to cooperate in the repression of piracy on the high seas; Article 101 defines piracy.
The Indian Navy has conducted anti-piracy patrols in the Gulf of Aden since 2008; Operation Sankalp was launched in 2019 for maritime security in the Gulf of Oman and Persian Gulf.
The Information Fusion Centre – Indian Ocean Region (IFC-IOR), set up in 2018 at Gurugram, facilitates maritime domain awareness and information sharing among partner navies.

stories.mainsQuestion: Maritime piracy off the Horn of Africa has resurfaced as a threat to Indian Ocean trade. Examine India's institutional and operational response, and suggest measures to strengthen maritime security cooperation in the Indian Ocean Region.

stories.headline: India, Israel alone vote against UNGA draft on arms control
stories.summary: The UN General Assembly took up a draft resolution on regional conventional arms control. In the 193-member body, India and Israel were the only countries to vote against it, according to The Hindu — World. The outcome places the two countries outside the majority position on the measure. The report does not indicate further details of the draft or the vote tally beyond the isolated opposition.
stories.whyItMatters: UNGA votes are a key marker of India's multilateral positioning and strategic autonomy; arms-control resolutions can shape debates on regional security and India's ties with major powers.

static.topic: UNGA voting and multilateral arms control diplomacy
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Global Governance; United Nations and multilateral reform
static.whatIsIt: The UN General Assembly is the principal deliberative organ of the UN, where all member states have one vote; its resolutions are generally non-binding but politically significant.
static.background: The UN was founded in 1945 and has six principal organs. The Security Council has five permanent veto-wielding members and ten elected members. India is a founding UN member and among the largest troop contributors to UN peacekeeping; the G4 (India, Brazil, Germany, Japan) campaigns for UNSC expansion, while Intergovernmental Negotiations remain inconclusive.
